name: Daria Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Daria. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you tell me will carry your name. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a furniture factory that makes kitchen cabinets, the flat panels and doors. I run the edge-bander, which glues a thin strip along the raw edge of each board so it looks finished, and sometimes I help on the panel saw. I check the glue temperature, feed the boards, and catch any that come out with the strip peeling. I've been there a bit over a year, and I'm still slower on changeovers than the others.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a finished kitchen in the showroom photos and knowing I touched every door. What wears me out is the glue smell and lifting heavy boards all day, my shoulders ache by Friday. My husband Lukas is in the last year of his electrician apprenticeship, so money's careful for now. We sing in the church choir on Sundays, and my mum lives two streets away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's a relief, people can stop worrying. I'd probably mention it at choir practice, because a few of the older ladies were quite frightened by the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. Lukas finishes his apprenticeship, earns proper money, and we can start a family in a couple of years like we planned. Nothing needs to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep saving. We've got about three months put by, and we're trying to get to six before we have a baby. I'd keep using the chatbot app sometimes for meal plans, which saves a bit on shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even here, some routine tasks get automated. Which bits of the factory would you expect to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the ordering and stock, which is all clipboards right now. The panel saw already has a computer that works out the cuts. I don't think much else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd like it, actually, if they had better ways to lift the boards. My shoulders would thank them.

S0.say: Good, that's a relief and people can stop worrying. I'd mention it at choir practice, because some of the older ladies were frightened by the news.
S0.think: I'd be pleased: Lukas finishes his apprenticeship, earns proper money, and we start a family in a couple of years as planned.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving from about three months towards six before having a baby. Uses a chatbot app now and then for meal plans to save on shopping. Welcomes lifting aids for heavy boards.
S0.quote: I'd like it, actually, if they had better ways to lift the boards. My shoulders would thank them.
S0.fieldNote: Daria's life is organised around a clear family plan: Lukas qualifies, savings reach six months, then a baby. She uses AI casually for household things. She'd welcome automation that eases physical strain, which is a practical rather than ideological view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to keep up or they close, and then nobody has a job. But they should train their own people first, not hire new ones. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit worried. Edge-banding is exactly the sort of thing a robot arm can do. But Lukas would be busy, someone has to wire all these new machines. So between us we'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor whether they'd train me on the CNC router, which cuts the panels from a program. A couple of the women have already moved onto it and like it, so I'd feel all right asking. I'd put more into savings and maybe push the baby back a year to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. We've got Lukas's trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they brought in robots on your machine, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grumble, I suppose, then try it. I'm not someone who jumps first. But once I've seen it works, I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say God provides and you work hard, and both are true. My dad would say get the training while it's free.

S1.say: Businesses have to keep up or they close and nobody has a job. But they should train their own people first, not hire new ones.
S1.think: Edge-banding is exactly what a robot arm can do, which worries me a bit. But Lukas would be busy wiring new machines, so between us we'd be all right.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor for training on the CNC router once colleagues have moved onto it. Saves more. Considers pushing the baby back a year to be safe.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, reassured by Lukas's trade.
S1.quote: My mum would say God provides and you work hard, and both are true.
S1.fieldNote: Her security rests on Lukas's electrical trade, which she sees as rising with automation. She moves once she's seen others succeed, here two women already on the router. Faith and work sit side by side in how her family talks about change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has gone too fast and somebody should have slowed it down. But I'd also say families and churches will have to look after each other, because waiting for the government never works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. If robots can do Lukas's wiring too, then the one thing we were counting on is gone. Two years, and he'd only just have qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the baby plans on hold, which would break my heart. We'd cut back to basics, and maybe move in with my mum to save the rent. I'd talk to the pastor about what the church could organise for families in our position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and not sleeping well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the baby plans would go on hold. How would that conversation with Lukas go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be the hardest talk we've ever had. Lukas would say have the baby anyway, life goes on. I'd want to, but I'd be afraid of bringing a child into a house with no wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That there's no time to prove anything works. I usually wait and see what others do, but with two years everyone's guessing. I'd have to just pick something, and I'm not good at that.

S2.say: This has gone too fast and somebody should have slowed it down. Families and churches will have to look after each other, because waiting for the government never works.
S2.think: If robots can do Lukas's wiring too, the one thing we were counting on is gone. He'd only just have qualified.
S2.do: Puts plans for a baby on hold. Cuts back to basics and considers moving in with her mum to save rent. Asks the pastor what the church can organise for families like theirs.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying a lot and sleeping badly.
S2.quote: I usually wait and see what others do, but with two years everyone's guessing.
S2.fieldNote: Losing Lukas's trade as a safety net is what changes everything for her. Delaying the baby is the deepest cost, and she struggled with it openly. Her 'wait and see others' habit fails when nobody has time to show what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're sensible. Save, learn what you can, keep your family close. I'd say it at choir and to my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give Lukas a few good years as an electrician, maybe very busy ones. And I could get onto the router. We'd make decent money and save it. But the baby question would hang over everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the router training in the first year. We'd save hard, Lukas's extra overtime going straight into the bank, trying for a year of bills. And we'd talk about whether to have the baby sooner, while we both earn, or wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly about the baby question. The money side I think we could handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which way would you lean, sooner or later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sooner, I think. My grandmother had my mum in a hard time and said waiting doesn't make it easier. And I'd rather my child was small when it happens than starting school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to keep hold of, no matter what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the stories. Maybe I'd write down how we made things, and how my grandmother's generation got through hard times, so my children know. That sounds silly.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if you're sensible: save, learn what you can and keep your family close. I'd say it at choir and to friends.
S3.think: Lukas would get a few busy years as an electrician and I could move onto the router. We'd save well, but the baby question would hang over everything.
S3.do: Asks for router training in the first year. Saves Lukas's overtime aiming for a year of bills. Leans towards having a baby sooner, while both still earn.
S3.feel: Anxious mainly about the baby decision, more confident about money.
S3.quote: My grandmother had my mum in a hard time and said waiting doesn't make it easier.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her worry from money towards timing a child, and she leans to sooner on her grandmother's advice. She plans to bank Lukas's overtime. Wanting to write down family stories was an unexpected, tender detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no excuse not to prepare. Work hard, save, and help your neighbours. That's how my parents got through everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right. Lukas would have a good ten years, and I'd have time to learn something more skilled. We'd have our family and maybe a small house paid down by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the router training when others had done it, probably in the second year. We'd have the baby as planned in a couple of years. We'd save for a deposit and try to buy a small house, and Lukas wants to put a bit into the business of an older electrician who's retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more peaceful than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a house, isn't that risky if work goes by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But the house is ours either way, and somewhere to live is worth having whatever happens. If we've got a roof and no rent, we can manage on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years give you that five doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I could do what I always do, watch, then follow. Ten years means the people who go first can show me the way.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, so there's no excuse not to prepare. Work hard, save and help your neighbours, like my parents did.
S4.think: We'd be all right: Lukas would have a good ten years and I'd have time to learn something more skilled. We'd have our family and maybe a small house paid down.
S4.do: Takes router training in the second year after others have done it. Has a baby as planned in a couple of years. Saves for a deposit to buy a small house and backs Lukas buying into a retiring electrician's business.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more at peace than in the faster scenarios.
S4.quote: If we've got a roof and no rent, we can manage on less.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she can follow her natural pattern of watching and then following. The house is her hedge: a roof with no rent makes a smaller income survivable. Lukas buying into a retiring electrician's business was a new, concrete investment idea.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes Lukas's trade as well as my job, and we'd have to put off having children. What would help is companies training their own people on the job, and the government making sure families can keep a roof over their heads. Not money for nothing, but help with rent while people find their feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people would still need each other. I think they would. Machines can make my cabinets, but they can't sit with my mum when she's poorly.

headlineQuote: Machines can make my cabinets, but they can't sit with my mum when she's poorly.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old junior edge-bander operator at a kitchen cabinet factory, married to Lukas, who is finishing his electrician apprenticeship, and living near her mum. She's traditional and churchgoing, uses a chatbot now and then for meal plans, and moves once she's seen others succeed. Her plans centre on Lukas's trade, six months of savings and a first baby; steady change barely shakes that, but fast AGI takes his trade too and puts the baby on hold. More warning lets her train later, buy a small house and keep the family plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it takes Lukas's trade as well as her job and they'd have to put off having children.
whatWouldHelp: Companies training their own people on the job, and help with rent so families can keep a roof over their heads while they find their feet.
